content.text: {"answers":[{"id":"p1","answer":"The tuple is converted into an `HTTPBasicAuth` object — the docs state that passing a `(username, password)` tuple is shorthand that is \"automatically converted into an HTTPBasicAuth object\" (docs/user/authentication.rst:26-33). The application happens in `PreparedRequest.prepare_auth(auth, url)` (src/requests/models.py:552-578 / 589-609), which invokes the handler's `__call__(r)`; `HTTPBasicAuth.__call__` sets `r.headers['Authorization'] = _basic_auth_str(self.username, self.password)` (src/requests/auth.py:111-113). `_basic_auth_str` (src/requests/auth.py:34-75) warns (DeprecationWarning) on non-string credentials and casts them, encodes `str` values to **latin1** bytes, joins them with a colon, base64-encodes the result, and prefixes it with `\"Basic \"` — giving `Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz`. The docs don't pin down the exact line where the tuple→HTTPBasicAuth coercion occurs, only that it happens during auth preparation."},{"id":"p2","answer":"The documentation only says that `prepare_body(data, files, json)` \"Encodes data/files, sets Content-Type and Content-Length\" (src/requests/models.py:484-521 / 503-587) — it does not document `prepare_content_length` or what it does when `body is None`, nor does it document that `prepare_auth` re-invokes it. So the documentation does not settle what the final body and Content-Length are. What can be said from the docs: `data={}` and `files=[]` carry no content to encode, so nothing is form- or multipart-encoded and the body shown in the trace is `None`; because the computation is driven solely by the body, calling it a second time from `prepare_auth` (after the Authorization header is added) recomputes the same value and is therefore harmless. Whether a `Content-Length: 0` header is emitted for a GET with a `None` body is not stated anywhere in the documentation provided."},{"id":"p3","answer":"It was computed by `requests.utils.get_encoding_from_headers(headers)` (src/requests/utils.py:532-555) from the response's `Content-Type` header, which it parses with `_parse_content_type_header` (src/requests/utils.py:507-529). With no `charset` parameter and a media type of `application/json`, the function returns `'utf-8'` (RFC 4627 default). Had the server sent `Content-Type: text/html` with no charset, the `'text' in media type` branch would have fired instead and it would have returned `'ISO-8859-1'` (the RFC 2616 default for text types)."},{"id":"p4","answer":"Because `r.encoding` was already set (to 'utf-8' from the header rules), `Response.json()` took the branch that simply decodes `Response.text` and hands it to `complexjson` (src/requests/models.py:968-1002); `guess_json_utf` (src/requests/utils.py:950-979) is only used as the fallback for detecting UTF-16/UTF-32 JSON when the encoding cannot otherwise be determined (see Content Encoding Detection). The exact guard condition for that fallback is not spelled out in the documentation. For a UTF-16 body while `encoding` is 'utf-8', the BOM/null-byte sniffing would be bypassed and the bytes would be decoded as UTF-8, producing garbage or a decode failure; the documented outcome of `Response.json()` failing to decode is `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError` (docs/api.rst:38), which subclasses `InvalidJSONError`/`RequestException` (src/requests/exceptions.py:42-43)."},{"id":"p5","answer":"The documentation provided does not document `HTTPAdapter.request_url` or its proxy logic — it is not in the adapter method tables (init_poolmanager, proxy_manager_for, cert_verify, build_response, get_connection_with_tls_context, send). What it does show is that the relative form comes from the `path_url` property supplied by `RequestEncodingMixin` (src/requests/models.py:108-204), and that proxies are resolved per-request via `select_proxy`/`resolve_proxies` and handled by a `ProxyManager` obtained from `proxy_manager_for` (src/requests/adapters.py:304-357). The standard behaviour of sending an absolute URI to a plain HTTP proxy is not stated in these docs, so I can't confirm from the documentation what it would have returned with a proxy configured."},{"id":"p6","answer":"The pool key always carries the TLS attributes so that connections with different verification settings are never shared (src/requests/adapters.py:375-423); with the default `verify=True`, `_urllib3_request_context` leaves certificate requirements at their default, i.e. `cert_reqs='CERT_REQUIRED'`, even though this particular request is plain HTTP. With `verify=False` it sets `cert_reqs='CERT_NONE'` (src/requests/adapters.py:98-99). With `verify='/path/to/ca.pem'` (an existing file) it sets `ca_certs='/path/to/ca.pem'` (src/requests/adapters.py:101-102); if the string were a directory it would set `ca_cert_dir` instead (src/requests/adapters.py:103-104). The docs don't explicitly state whether `cert_reqs` remains `CERT_REQUIRED` alongside `ca_certs`, though nothing in them changes it. The default CA material itself comes from `certifi` via `requests.certs.where()` (src/requests/certs.py:15-18)."},{"id":"p8","answer":"The documentation does not cover this case. It only documents the 2-tuple shorthand `(username, password)` being converted into `HTTPBasicAuth` (docs/user/authentication.rst:26-33) and otherwise describes `auth` as an `AuthBase` subclass / callable applied by `prepare_auth` (src/requests/models.py:552-578, src/requests/auth.py:78-82). A 3-tuple matches neither documented form, so nothing in the docs tells us whether it is rejected, silently ignored, or passed through to be called as a handler; I'd have to read the code to say."},{"id":"g1","answer":"The documentation describes `prepare_cookies(cookies)` only as converting cookies into the `Cookie` header via `get_cookie_header` (src/requests/models.py:539-550 / 610-628); it does not state any guarantee (or restriction) about calling it more than once, so I can't confirm the once-only contract from these docs. What the docs do say about redirects is that `SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects` builds a **new** `PreparedRequest` for each redirect target rather than mutating the original in place (src/requests/sessions.py:186-290), and that session cookies are re-extracted from each response with `extract_cookies_to_jar` (src/requests/sessions.py:27). The consequence for reusing a single `PreparedRequest` object across sends is not documented here."},{"id":"g2","answer":"A `Session` keeps `self.adapters` as an `OrderedDict` mapping URL prefix → adapter, pre-populated with `'http://'` and `'https://'` HTTPAdapters (src/requests/sessions.py:433-440, 465-470). On send it iterates the adapters and selects the one whose prefix is the **longest match** for the target URL (src/requests/sessions.py:748-755); `Session.mount(prefix, adapter)` registers new ones (src/requests/sessions.py:804-812). The misuse this invites: matching is on the URL string prefix, not on a parsed host, so a mount like `'https://example.com'` also matches look-alike URLs that merely start with that string (e.g. `https://example.com.attacker.net/`), and a URL whose scheme matches no prefix raises `InvalidSchema` (src/requests/exceptions.py:114-116). The prefix-vs-host pitfall is an inference from the documented matching rule; the docs don't call it out explicitly."},{"id":"g3","answer":"`SessionRedirectMixin.should_strip_auth(old_url, new_url)` (src/requests/sessions.py:154-184) returns True — and the `Authorization` header is dropped — when the hostname changes, or when the port changes. The deliberately allowed case is the standard HTTP→HTTPS upgrade on default ports (same host, 80 → 443), which does not strip auth. Separately, `Proxy-Authorization` is always stripped on redirect because proxy auth is hop-by-hop/connection-specific (src/requests/sessions.py:253)."},{"id":"g4","answer":"They act as the environment-level source for the CA bundle path and are folded in by `Session.merge_environment_settings()` / `resolve_proxies`-style merging (src/requests/sessions.py:711-715, 76-105). Precedence is: method-level argument > session attribute > environment variable, so an explicit `verify=` wins. `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` is the primary variable and `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` is the fallback when it is unset (docs/user/advanced.rst:238-239). They are ignored when the session has `trust_env=False`, and — importantly — when you build a `PreparedRequest` yourself and call `Session.send()` directly, since environment settings are not merged automatically; you must call `s.merge_environment_settings(prepped.url, {}, None, None, None)` and pass the result into `send()` (docs/user/advanced.rst:190-207)."},{"id":"g5","answer":"By default an `HTTPAdapter` does not retry: `DEFAULT_RETRIES` is 0 (src/requests/adapters.py:81), and `max_retries` is documented as \"the maximum number of retries each connection should attempt\" (src/requests/adapters.py:168). So `max_retries=0` means a connection-level failure surfaces immediately as an exception, while `max_retries=3` has urllib3 retry the connection up to three times before giving up (exhausting retries is what the `RetryError` exception represents, src/requests/exceptions.py). Note that the `timeout` value applies to *each* attempt, so wall-clock time grows with retries (docs/user/advanced.rst:479-482). For finer control you pass a `urllib3.util.retry.Retry` object, e.g. `HTTPAdapter(max_retries=Retry(total=3, read=False))`. The documentation here doesn't spell out which failure classes the integer form covers beyond \"each connection\"."},{"id":"g6","answer":"Requests uses `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` when the request body is a generator or iterator whose length cannot be determined — specifically an object without a `__len__()` method passed as `data` (docs/user/advanced.rst:368-380). The length determination is done by `requests.utils.super_len` (src/requests/utils.py:160-251), which tries `__len__`, a `len` attribute, `fstat(fileno())`, or `tell()/seek()`; if none yields a size, the body is streamed chunked rather than given a `Content-Length`. Plain file objects opened in binary mode do get a `Content-Length` and are streamed un-chunked (docs/user/advanced.rst:348-364). The decision is made during `prepare_body` (src/requests/models.py:484-521); the adapter then performs the chunked send. Malformed chunked *responses* raise `ChunkedEncodingError`."},{"id":"g7","answer":"`HTTPAdapter.send` catches urllib3/socket-level failures and re-raises them as requests exceptions (src/requests/adapters.py:19-50, 448-614). The mappings the documentation states explicitly are: `urllib3.exceptions.ConnectTimeoutError` → `requests.exceptions.ConnectTimeout`; `urllib3.exceptions.ReadTimeoutError` → `requests.exceptions.ReadTimeout`; `urllib3.exceptions.SSLError` → `requests.exceptions.SSLError`; and generic urllib3/socket/DNS failures → `requests.exceptions.ConnectionError` (see the error-flow sequence in the Error Handling page). `ProxyError` and `InvalidProxyURL` cover proxy failures and malformed proxy URLs, `RetryError` covers exhausted retry logic, `ContentDecodingError` a failed decompression, and `ChunkedEncodingError` a malformed chunked body (src/requests/exceptions.py:70-148). The precise urllib3 source classes for the latter group (ProtocolError, DecodeError, MaxRetryError, etc.) are not named in the documentation provided."}]}
